findings.quote: In humans, a male has only one allele for a gene on the X chromosome.
findings.problem: This generalization fails for genes in the pseudoautosomal regions. An XY male has two copies of these genes, one on X and one on Y. Students applying this rule would incorrectly count their alleles.

findings.quote: In a very large group, luck averages out and drift is small, though never exactly zero.
findings.problem: Drift does not guarantee a nonzero frequency change. At a fixed locus, every copy is the same allele, so random sampling cannot change its frequency. Even at a variable locus, a generation can retain exactly the previous frequency by chance.
findings.source: [OpenStax, Concepts of Biology, 11.2 Mechanisms of Evolution: Genetic Drift](https://openstax.org/books/concepts-biology/pages/11-2-mechanisms-of-evolution)

findings.quote: Individuals may change during life, but changes gained during life are not passed on. A mutation in the DNA that offspring receive is the exception.
findings.problem: Mutation is not the only exception. Some acquired changes can pass to offspring through non-DNA-sequence inheritance. Experiments in C. elegans demonstrated an acquired antiviral response transmitted across generations through small RNAs. The categorical rule wrongly excludes this inheritance.
findings.source: [Rechavi, Minevich and Hobert (2011), Transgenerational inheritance of an acquired small RNA-based antiviral response in C. elegans, Cell](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22119442/)
